data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":["SRC_005","SRC_007"],"disanalogies":["A single evaluation can test causal structure if it includes an active intervention, contradicting the claim that a single evaluation is limited to observation.","Mere compliance is typically defined as behavioral adherence, whereas here it is operationalized as statistical coupling to spurious features."],"overturn_conditions":["The evaluation environment is strictly stationary, making causal and correlational features indistinguishable.","The cost or feasibility of generating an adversarial evaluation set is prohibitive, rendering the interventionist criterion practically void."],"shared_structure":["The necessity of causal anchoring to distinguish structural reliability from spurious tracking.","The use of distribution shift or intervention to test causal vs. correlational structure.","The rejection of the claim that a single static evaluation cannot distinguish these modes."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_005","SRC_007"],"transfer_claims":["The causal inference framework's interventionist criterion transfers directly: if manipulating a checklist feature changes the panel's judgment but not the outcome, the panel's reliability is mere compliance.","The failure mode of mere compliance is a characteristic collapse of accuracy under distribution shift, which is observable in a single evaluation if the evaluation set is designed adversarially."]},"claim":"Within a single evaluation, genuine reliability gain is distinguished from mere checklist compliance by exposing the system to an adversarial distribution shift where superficial checklist features are decorrelated from the outcome; a genuine gain relies on causally anchored features, whereas mere compliance catastrophically fails.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The checklist explicitly encodes all causative features, making the distinction between 'compliance' and 'genuine gain' trivial and identical in effect.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The domain expert's intuition is also trained on spurious correlations, in which case both systems fail under distribution shift and the evaluation is non-distinguishing.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The covering principle is the necessity of causal anchoring for out-of-distribution robustness. A single evaluation can distinguish causal structure from spurious correlation by actively intervening on the domain. If the panel's reliability is mere compliance, its judgments are structurally coupled to the checklist's explicit features. If those features are non-causative but historically correlated, an adversarial intervention that breaks this correlation will cause the panel's accuracy to plummet while a domain expert relying on true causal intuition (or a checklist with causative features) maintains performance. The distinguishing evidence is the divergence of accuracy trajectories under this controlled perturbation.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
